title: Northstar Home Systems: scaling a connected heating-controls range
narrative:
Northstar Home Systems Ltd is a Leeds-based manufacturer and online seller of smart heating controls for UK households. It employs 186 people and generated revenue of £8.4m in the year ended March 2026. Its main product, the Halo thermostat, is assembled in Leeds from imported circuit boards, UK-made casings and bought-in sensors. Northstar’s objective is to grow Halo sales while protecting product reliability and avoiding further pressure on cash.

Demand for Halo has increased after large energy retailers began listing it online. Forecast sales for the next 12 months are 52,000 units, compared with 39,000 units in the previous year. However, the forecast assumes that retailers’ promotions continue and that competing low-priced products do not reduce Northstar’s selling price. The operations director believes the existing packing line will not reliably handle peak weekly demand. The board is considering an automated packing line, which would also provide serial-number scanning for traceability and reduce manual packing errors.

Northstar currently has a five-layer functional hierarchy. Production, purchasing, sales and finance managers report to the operations director, who refers significant decisions to the managing director. Most production staff have permanent full-time contracts and work to detailed procedures. Managers say this structure has helped quality control, but team leaders report slow decisions when shortages occur. The proposed change would remove one management layer, create multi-skilled production cells and give cell leaders authority to alter daily staffing and production schedules within agreed quality and spending limits. Some supervisors fear redundancy or loss of status; some assemblers are concerned about learning new tasks and being measured through the new scanning system. The managing director has announced the intended launch date but has not yet decided whether to use a pilot, consultation meetings, training, or a faster compulsory implementation.

Northstar’s March management accounts showed an operating profit of £504,000, but its closing cash balance was only £96,000. Customers, including retailers, usually pay 60 days after delivery, while Northstar pays its main circuit-board supplier 30 days after invoice. Inventory has risen from £610,000 to £1.05m as purchasing staff ordered larger batches to avoid shortages. The finance director’s rolling forecast shows a possible cash shortfall in July if £420,000 of retailer receipts arrive two weeks late. Management is considering tighter customer-credit control, selling surplus slow-moving casings, negotiating longer supplier terms, reducing buffer stock, delaying the packing-line purchase or using an overdraft. Each option could affect customer relationships, supplier reliability, output or future growth.

The circuit boards currently come from one supplier in Malaysia. Its unit price is £18.40 and its normal lead time is 10 weeks; it requires minimum orders of 12,000 boards. A UK supplier has offered boards at £20.10 each, in batches of 3,000, with a three-week lead time. The UK supplier has spare capacity but has supplied Northstar only on a small trial order. A recent port delay added three weeks to a Malaysian delivery, causing Northstar to use almost all of its buffer inventory. A missed delivery of Halo thermostats would expose Northstar to retailer penalties and may damage online customer ratings. The purchasing manager argues that the Malaysian supplier remains cheaper; the sales director argues that lower inventory, shorter lead times and dual sourcing could be worth the higher purchase price.

To decide how to secure circuit-board supply for the coming winter peak, Northstar has estimated outcomes using internal data. If it continues with the Malaysian supplier alone, managers estimate a 0.70 probability of normal supply, producing an expected seasonal contribution of £780,000, and a 0.30 probability of a serious delay, producing a contribution of £270,000 after lost sales and expedited freight. Establishing a dual-source arrangement would cost £95,000 in testing, supplier onboarding and revised quality checks. Under dual sourcing, management estimates a 0.85 probability of normal supply with seasonal contribution before these costs of £745,000, and a 0.15 probability of a serious delay with contribution before these costs of £510,000. The estimates are based on Northstar’s experience and supplier discussions rather than independently verified probabilities.

The automated packing-line project must be ready before the retailer promotion begins. The project manager has listed the activities and dependencies below. The engineering contractor has offered to shorten activity E by two weeks for an additional £36,000, but this would require weekend access to the factory. The operations director also wants to know whether the project schedule alone is sufficient, since the same maintenance technicians are needed for normal production and for installing the line.
